scope_note: Authoritative family-recognition backfill for the Hays/Central Texas learner. Canonical native lesson is built from Berberis trifoliolata and Berberis swaseyi; Mahonia source rows are preserved as historical synonym records; Nandina domestica is retained only as a labeled invasive comparison; Berberis aquifolium is an out-of-range encounter/horticultural comparison.

family_lesson.where_to_look_first: For the local native lesson, start with an evergreen prickly shrub with yellow wood and compound leaves with stiff spine-tipped leaflet margins. In flower, look for a many-part petaloid perianth, 6 nectar-bearing petals, 6 stamens opposite the petals, a superior one-carpellate ovary, and in Berberis anthers that open by two hinged valves.
family_lesson.strongest_field_confirmation: Local Berberis: bright yellow inner wood/tissue + leathery spiny leaflets + small yellow flowers + 6 stamens whose anthers open by apically hinged valves + berry fruit.
core_characters: Berberidaceae includes woody shrubs and perennial herbs; our local native anchors are evergreen shrubs.
Leaves generally alternate; they may be simple, pinnately compound, or ternately compound.
Perianth is free and multiseriate; sepals are often petaloid and occur in multiple whorls.
Petals usually 6 and often bear paired nectar glands or nectaries near the base in Berberis.
Stamens commonly 6 and opposite the petals.
Anther dehiscence is highly diagnostic but not uniform across the family: Berberis uses two apically hinged valves; Nandina opens by longitudinal slits.
Ovary superior and usually one-carpellate in the family framework.
Fruit may be a berry or capsule; local Berberis and Nandina both produce berries.
avoid_overgeneralizing: Do not teach valve-opening anthers as universal for Berberidaceae; Nandina opens its anthers by longitudinal slits.
Do not teach the perianth simply as '6 tepals'; local Berberis has multiple petaloid sepal whorls plus 6 nectar-bearing petals.
Do not keep Mahonia swaseyi and Mahonia trifoliolata as separate modern learner taxa; current POWO places them in Berberis.
Do not identify Berberis swaseyi by leaflet count alone because it hybridizes with B. trifoliolata in Central Texas.
Do not count Nandina domestica or Berberis aquifolium toward project-native metrics.

fastest_cues: Leaves consistently 3-foliolate in the clean species concept.
Three stiff blue-green leaflets with strong spine-tipped lobes/teeth.
Fragrant yellow flowers clustered at nodes.
Berberis trifoliolata.reproductive_cue: Classic Berberis flower with 6 petals, 6 stamens and valvate anther dehiscence.
Berberis trifoliolata.hybrid_warning: Central Texas plants may hybridize with B. swaseyi, so leaflet count alone is not sufficient for every individual.

fastest_cues: Berries white or red, often glaucous, 9–16 mm, frequently hollow.
Berberis swaseyi.reproductive_cue: Anther filaments have a distal pair of recurved lateral teeth in FNA; flower/stamen micromorphology helps separate pure B. swaseyi from hybrids.
Berberis swaseyi.conservation_note: TPWD lists Berberis swaseyi as a Species of Greatest Conservation Need, G3/S3.

hybrid_lesson.local_importance: Documented at the Purola Preserve/Hays County flora site; dozens of putative hybrids have been recognized there.
hybrid_lesson.why_it_matters: This is an excellent learner example of why a single easy character such as leaflet number can fail.
hybrid_lesson.practical_rule: Use leaflet architecture as a first clue, then inspect inflorescence bracteoles, fruit, and especially stamen morphology when a plant is intermediate.

comparison_taxa.status: non-native invasive comparison; exclude from native metrics
key_traits: Leaves 2–3 times pinnately compound with many entire leaflets.
Large terminal/axillary panicles of small white flowers.
Six stamens, but anthers open by longitudinal slits rather than hinged valves.
Native to China; introduced in Texas and listed by TexasInvasives.
comparison_taxa.teaching_value: Shows why valvate anthers and spiny leaflets describe local Berberis, not every member of Berberidaceae.

key_traits: Evergreen compound-leaved Berberis formerly widely called Mahonia aquifolium.
Native range is southwestern Canada to northern California.

visual_sequence: one petal with its opposite/adnate-looking stamen relationship
anther with paired hinged valves lifted open
Berberis.special_behavior: Berberis stamens are touch-sensitive/irritable and can move inward toward the pistil when stimulated. This is useful enrichment, but should not replace structural ID characters.
Berberis.local_source: UT Austin Hays Flora Berberis stamen-morphology series.

Nandina.contrast: Numerous sepals/perianth parts and 6 stamens, but anthers dehisce by longitudinal slits. Use as the family-exception card.

fruit_lesson.Berberis trifoliolata: Bright red berry, usually solid; strong field cue with 3-foliolate leaves.
fruit_lesson.Berberis swaseyi: White to red somewhat glaucous berry, commonly larger and often hollow.
fruit_lesson.Nandina domestica: Globose red berry with 1–3 seeds; invasive comparison only.

Ranunculaceae.confusion: Both are in Ranunculales and can have numerous-looking free perianth parts and superior ovaries.
Ranunculaceae.tie_breaker: Local Berberis is a woody evergreen spiny shrub with compound leathery leaves, yellow wood, 6 petals with nectaries and valvate anthers; local Ranunculaceae is generally herbaceous or vine-like and lacks that woody/spiny/yellow-wood combination.

Rosaceae.confusion: Woody shrubs with 5-ish to many visible perianth parts and fleshy fruit can look superficially similar.
Rosaceae.tie_breaker: Rosaceae commonly shows a hypanthium and numerous stamens; local Berberis has 6 stamens opposite 6 petals and valvate anthers, plus bright yellow wood and spiny compound foliage.
